articles.title: Phantom Blade Zero Doesn’t Have an Achievement for Beating Its Hardest Mode; A Growing Trend in the Games Industry Is to Blame
articles.summary: There's no achievement for beating Phantom Blade Zero's most difficult mode, and trophy hunters are to blame.
articles.body:
This is an opinion piece from writer Travis Northup. IGN's opinion columns represent the personal viewpoints of the writer, drawing on their own experiences and research to explore the exciting world of video games.

During a recent visit to Phantom Blade Zero developer S-GAME ahead of the action RPG’s release, the studio showed off a pretty neat difficulty option that unlocks once you’ve beaten the game, called 66 Days Mode. Here, you’re given just 66 chances to complete the entire campaign, turning the protagonist’s heart condition into a smart in-game mechanic for truly dedicated players to take on as the ultimate challenge. Excitedly, another member of the press said, “Ooh, that’ll be a fun achievement to chase,” to which a developer quickly chimed in to say, “No, no. There’s no achievement. All achievements can be acquired on a single playthrough on any difficulty.”

This is a strategy I’ve heard quite a few times in 2026. Over the course of my numerous game studio visits this year, I’ve spoken with more and more developers who are intentionally curating their achievements list to be as approachable and inoffensive as possible. Why? Because they’ve learned that there’s a growing population of players who factor them into their purchasing decision – sometimes even opting to skip out on games they would have otherwise enjoyed if collecting all of the digital trophies isn’t a guarantee, or requires them to go out of their way.

The result of this threatens a landscape that’s worse for everyone, whether it’s players who have become increasingly invested in the treadmill of chores to complete or developers who have a financial incentive to design components of their game around the desires of the achievement-hunting community (undermining the entire point of achievements to begin with).

Achievements have, of course, been around since the Xbox 360 debuted in 2005. Within three years, both PlayStation and Steam had their own equivalents. Yet despite being well aware of their two-decade existence and the obsession that can surround them, I’d never personally talked to anyone from the achievement-hunting caucus until recently. I made a new acquaintance while playing tabletop RPGs, and while making small talk during character creation, I noticed this person had a Steam Deck with them. I asked what games they were excited about playing, and they said, “I’m thinking of getting the new Castlevania game… just waiting to see what the achievements list looks like.” I used the opportunity to probe into their worldview and how they enjoy games. They explained that for them, checking off the list of to-dos in a game was cathartic, and if too much was required of them to complete the list, it stressed them out and made them not want to play at all.

For as long as RPGs and quest logs have existed, there’s certainly been an element of the checklist and completionism in the nerd space, as many of us have a compulsion to do and see everything a game offers. That’s now a part of game design more than ever thanks to the growth of live-service: Fortnite wants you to log in daily to tick off a list of jobs that may not even be in the game modes you want to play that day, but you do so just to receive that hit of XP. That influence has bled over into offline single-player games as well, like Ubisoft adding an in-game list of daily and weekly chores to tick off in recent Assassin’s Creed games, asking you to unnecessarily grind repetitive tasks rather than focusing on the more engaging content those games offer.

I’ve always considered those dailies as optional extras at best and chaff to be ignored at worst. So I’d be lying if I said it isn’t at least a little bit depressing to hear that, for some, the medium has been reduced to a Trello-like task board that they prepare for in advance and play while heavily referencing a guide to ensure they don’t miss out on any of the trophies along the way. For me, the whole point of gaming as a medium is discovery, experiencing your own personal version of an adventure or story, and, well, playing . It feels like a growing number of players have forgotten the playing part – like those who follow the instructions on a LEGO set step-by-step rather than using those building blocks to create something unique.

While I don’t believe this approach of play is anywhere close to becoming mainstream, it’s clearly dominant enough that it’s affecting the design strategy behind achievements and even games at large. Not including an achievement for a game’s hardest task for fear of alienating a particular group, or calibrating an entire achievement list to be easily attained on a single playthrough completely inverts the entire point of achievements, where players were incentivized to hunt for secrets and overcome the most challenging content. Not only that, if this strategy becomes widespread over time, it will have taken something that’s supposed to be fun and turned it into something that exists purely as a marketing tool for the developer. “How painless will it be to get all the achievements?” becomes just another bullet on some PR manager’s press release to persuade those with an acquired addiction to these virtual badges to spend time and money on their game. I certainly have my own opinions of those who place so much stock in achievements that they allow them to determine which games they play, but even those who casually enjoy aiming for the highest accolades and hunting for the most elusive secrets have lost something when achievements for pursuing those challenges no longer exist.

But there’s a much more consequential issue at play here: how the habits of achievement hunters are actively affecting game development. It seems that many developers actually designing the games aren’t as thrilled by it. I’ve begun asking designers and directors about their relationship with achievements any chance I get, and the most common sentiments from my limited sample range from mild annoyance to outright antagonism toward them.

Sam Barlow, a designer who worked on the Silent Hill series before creating indie darlings like Her Story and Immortality, recently took to social media to express his opinion on the matter, writing a thread of posts that describes the friction quite well:

And herein lies the problem: when players start taking achievements seriously, especially if it’s factoring into which games they choose to buy, developers have to start taking them seriously too. And if they want to use achievements to encourage players to chase interesting stuff they’ve hidden in their game or take down its most challenging content, as most developers I’ve talked to seem to want, then they find themselves at odds with the “easy checklist” a segment of players are looking for. Now what was a minor annoyance that non-achievement hunters could mostly ignore has real consequences for all of us – because the fear of losing out on the market of achievement hunters could actively influence actual game design.

In Phantom Blade Zero’s case, the impact on design is pretty clear, as S-GAME has stated that the 66 Days Mode has no unique weapons, enemies, or unlockables associated with it – not even a fun cosmetic item for those who beat it to show off. It’s definitely possible that there are completely unrelated reasons for this decision, but my conversations with the team certainly made it seem like not pissing off the achievement hunters was at least part of the reason here.

There’s an interesting argument to be made where one could view this shift in achievement philosophy as a move toward accessibility and not placing these accolades out of reach for those who don’t have the time, patience, or skill to do the demanding stuff that’s sometimes required. It’s certainly an angle I’ve heard some developers focus on when they describe their approach, including some of the developers at S-GAME in regard to Phantom Blade Zero. And there’s likely a genuine effort by some to simply remove barriers for those who care about achievements – a small price to pay to appease those who do, especially when most developers don’t seem to. But that shift also removes any sense of real achievement for those who do want challenging or interesting objectives beyond those presented within a game.

And in any case, if accessibility is a factor, it’s certainly secondary to the thing game makers actually care about: selling their game to as many people as possible. Whether you think it’s a good thing or not, you have no incentive to play Phantom Blade Zero’s 66 Days Mode aside from your own satisfaction, and that’s at least partially influenced by the commoditization of achievements as a selling point rather than a fun list of optional pursuits. And if achievements no longer exist as digital bragging rights for exactly the type of pursuit that 66 Days Mode represents, then what purpose do they serve?

Maybe this new era of challenge-free achievements is just the invisible hand of the market doing its thing. Maybe developers, who could use some help avoiding studio closure and layoffs these days, will be able to benefit from those who care about achievements by selling a few extra copies. But whether it’s the clinical way a growing number of players are using achievement lists as glorified Jira tasks, the vanishing number of achievements that are actually worthy of bragging about, or the impact of achievement-hunting culture on the actual development of games, it seems to be making things worse for all of us. And I, for one, think that’s a shame for something that started out so intentionally silly and fun.

Travis Northup is a writer for IGN. You can follow him on Twitter @TieGuyTravis and read his games coverage here .

articles.title: GTA 6 Now the Most Preordered Game in PlayStation Store and Microsoft Store History, Official Preload Warning Issued
articles.summary: Sony has confirmed that GTA 6 is now the most preordered game in PlayStation Store history, although it failed to put a number on it. Microsoft hasn’t made an announcement on GTA 6 preorders for Xbox Series X and S.
articles.body:
Sony has confirmed that GTA 6 is now the most preordered game in PlayStation Store history, although it failed to put a number on it.

In a post on the PlayStation Blog , Sony Interactive Entertainment Content Communications Manager, Tim Turi, said Sony had seen “unprecedented demand” for Rockstar’s next game. Preload is now live ahead of the rolling midnight launch by country ( we’ve got the global release times right here ) from November 19.

According to data from sales tracking firm Sensor Tower , GTA 6 has already "sold" 9.69 million units, suggesting it's the most preordered game of all time, surpassing CD Projekt's Cyberpunk 2077. This week, Rockstar parent company Take-Two said GTA 6 preorders were tracking "far in excess of our initial expectations, and we know that the numbers will speak for themselves soon enough." According to Take-Two, some gamers are saving their money for GTA 6, skipping recent releases in the process .

Similarly, Microsoft has now confirmed that GTA 6 is the most preordered title of all time on the Microsoft Store. The company today confirmed GTA 6 will be playable on Xbox Series X and S and even Xbox One via Cloud Gaming , but not PC or mobile. Microsoft also announced it will add more Rockstar games to Xbox Cloud Gaming, including Grand Theft Auto 5, Red Dead Redemption 2, in the coming months.

Sony and Microsoft both issued a warning that fans should preload the game as soon as possible, perhaps mindful of the weight of demand that is heading the their online stores next week.

“Given the anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, we strongly advise that everyone who is hoping to play on launch day to preload the game as soon as possible,” Turi said. “Players who purchased the code-in-box version can also activate their code as soon as they get it to begin preloading. If you still haven’t pre-ordered the game, now’s the time to do so to make sure you’re ready for November 19.”

Today’ Rockstar finally confirmed some of the performance specs for GTA 6 , including exclusive PS5 Pro graphics features. Essentially, GTA 6 is targeting 30fps across all consoles, including Xbox Series S.

On PS5, GTA 6 includes integrated speakers, haptic feedback and adaptive triggers across the game through DualSense wireless controllers, and adjustable via accessibility settings. “All in-game sounds take full advantage of Tempest 3D Audio for highly accurate audio positioning, while load times are improved with PS5’s ultra high-speed SSD, making Grand Theft Auto VI play best on PlayStation 5 consoles,” Sony said.

articles.title: GTA 6 Fans Are Divided Over Confirmation of 30fps
articles.summary: GTA 6 will be 30fps, creating division among fans and frustration for PS5 Pro owners.
articles.body:
GTA 6 will be 30fps, creating division among fans and frustration for PS5 Pro owners.

Rockstar Games confirmed today that GTA 6 will target 30fps on all consoles , including PS5 Pro. This answers one of the biggest questions that has surrounded the game for years, but the answer also likely isn't a big surprise to many. Given the scope and scale of this game, as well as Rockstar's history with other games, a lot of people assumed this would be a 30fps game. However, there was hope that PS5 Pro would offer 60fps, or at least a 40fps mode as a compromise.

Still, the confirmation is creating all kinds of waves across social media. Some fans are pretty understanding, noting that the trade-off for a lower frame rate is an extremely dense, visually intense game.

"It's a shame they could not get it running at 40-60fps, and it would’ve been way better to play at 60fps, but I also fully understand why this happened," said one fan . "You don’t get to make the most dense, detailed, and graphically intensive game of the generation without making sacrifices."

"GTA 6 has a ton of complex systems running at once and reaching that level of realism while maintaining a stable framerate is impossible due to the CPU bottleneck," explained another fan . "Rockstar Games probably had to choose between cutting down complex systems like NPC density, NPC AI, Cars, Random Events etc. for a higher framerate or keeping those while targeting 30FPS to reach the highest level of realism possible and now we know that they went with the latter."

"30fps in [Red Dead Redemption 2] is good enough," stated a user on X . "As long as input latency is lower and there are no significant frame drops, I think GTA 6 will be alright."

Others are not as generous, however. One fan refunded the Ultimate Edition of GTA 6, noting they'll wait for the inevitable PS6 version that will likely have performance enhancements, possibly including 60fps. A big part of the frustration comes from people who expected more out of the PS5 Pro. Some fans shelled out a lot of extra money for the console, assuming it would give them a notable leap in quality from the base console. While it will have some exclusive features, like ray-traced shadows and PSSR, it's not the jump that some were hoping for.

"People paid over a grand for slightly better upscaling + ray-tracing but still the same 30 fps performance," said a user on X .

"I understand that the game is massive, and that this was (probably) the only way it would’ve even been playable on a console, but damn," said another fan . "It’s 2026. 30fps?! I’m losing excitement for GTA 6 by the day."

"60fps is the floor for modern titles on PS5 Pro and above, not 30...but Rockstar are dragging us back a good 5-10 years here," said an annoyed fan on Reddit . "They knew the hardware capabilities, and chose to make a game that isn't really compatible with it...that's what's crazy here."

Another fan pointed out there may also be some hypocrisy regarding this situation, as games like Starfield have been panned for being 30fps: "No offense towards GTA 6 it will be good, but Starfield got assaulted for being locked to 30fps and runs at 60fps on Xbox and PS5 now, are we gonna have the same energy for GTA 6 being locked to 30fps?"

Many games offer some kind of performance mode to unlock higher frame rates, at the cost of a lower resolution, a lack of ray-tracing, or other compromises. However, it doesn't seem like GTA 6 will have that, much to the annoyance of some fans. Maybe there's a chance Rockstar will add some performance buffs post-launch, but I wouldn't hold my breath. Red Dead Redemption 2 has been stuck at 30fps on consoles since 2018.

There are rumors that a GTA 6 PC port will arrive in early 2027, which would likely be the definitive version of the game with much higher frame rates. Rockstar has yet to confirm any platforms for the game beyond Xbox and PlayStation (though you can play the game on Xbox One through the cloud ), but maybe we'll hear more about a potential PC version in the new year.

Despite some division over performance options, GTA 6 is just nine days away from launch, and the hype is at its peak. Players can pre-load the game starting today , which they absolutely should if they want to play it as soon as it is available. The game will take up nearly 212 GBs, so it may take a while to download, depending on internet speeds. PlayStation and Xbox have also both confirmed that the game is the most pre-ordered title in their respective histories, meaning this game is likely going to shatter all kinds of sales records next week.

Cade Onder is a freelancer for IGN's news team. He covers all things entertainment, including gaming, film, and more. You can find him on Twitter @Cade_Onder.

articles.title: The indie game community is in disarray over AI and Big Walk
articles.summary: Some IGF jurors will not vote for games that use generative AI in “any capacity.” Big Walk developer House House said it “sparingly” used AI in the “final stretch” of the game’s development.
articles.body: Some Independent Games Festival (IGF) jurors published a statement yesterday saying they would not vote for games that use generative AI in “any capacity.” Soon after, the developer of indie hit Big Walk has published a statement saying it “sparingly” used AI in the “final stretch” of the game’s development to “help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs.” According to the jurors’ statement, a copy of which was posted by Austin Walker, while this year’s IGF entries have been “incredible,” there has been “a significant increase” in the number of games “developed with generative AI tools,” leading to “fairly intense discussion and disagreement” with no “universal consensus.” The statement includes a list of beliefs, including that generative AI has “negative effects,” that AI-generated code is “not an exception to these harms,” and that use of AI tools is “not a forgone conclusion in our industry.” IGF jurors that signed include Telling Lies and Immortality creator Sam Barlow and Celeste composer Lena Raine. The jurors say that the statement doesn’t speak for IGF as an organization or for all IGF jury members, noting that some voiced concern about being able to safely sign “without professional blowback.” [Media: One contentious title was apparently Big Walk, the co-op adventure game from Untitled Goose Game developer House House. In a statement to Aftermath and posted on its website, House House said that “In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code—we’d estimate that well under 0.1% of Big Walk’s code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game.” House House said its “primary use case” of LLMs was “to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code,” including fixing an issue with shadows by modifying LLM-suggested code. House House noted it turned to the “LLM chatbot” after researching the problem “extensively” and even speaking to an engineer at Unity. The studio said it disclosed its AI usage as part of its IGF submission, though it has not disclosed AI usage on Big Walk’s Steam page because “the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage.” “This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal,” House House said. “We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as ‘inevitable’. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to videogames and our world, and apologise that Big Walk’s LLM usage may not meet their standards.” House House didn’t have an AI policy in place when it developed Big Walk, which it described as a “failure,” and said it will “work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards.” Barlow said after we published this post that Big Walk was not the “impetus” for the IGF’s discussion, but it became the “tricky edge case — well what about this minimal use of AI, what about when your favorite game, or team uses it?” Barlow added that “This is not a call to boycott a certain game, or to economically hurt a team — this was about a single award’s show of many and what that award should mean to reflect our ‘indie’ alternative to mainstream and larger scale game development.” Walker also shared a long blog post that’s worth reading about his position on AI and the IGF awards. [Media: Update, November 10th: Added posts from Barlow and Walker.

articles.title: Logitech Is Letting Employees Take Work Off for Game Releases, Just Ahead of GTA 6
articles.summary: Logitech has announced that it will be giving employees the option to take time off for video game releases ahead of GTA 6's launch.
articles.body:
Logitech has announced that it will be giving employees the option to take time off for video game releases ahead of GTA 6's launch.

The tech company announced that it will label this perk as "Logi Game Day" for its employees. Logitech explained that this idea came about from an internal study, which concluded that "81% of gamers believe that gaming builds real-world confidence, reduces anxiety, and correlates with stronger day-to-day work performance." Another study noted that 98.8% of enterprise ITDM respondents believe that gaming translates to actual workplace skills, such as problem-solving and acting under pressure.

As a result, the company is going to lean into that and give people the freedom to take time off to play new video games.

“It’s time to retire the stereotype that gaming is a waste of time,” said Hanneke Faber, Logitech’s chief executive officer. “As a company designing products for work and play, we see every day how engagement in one sphere supports performance in the other.”

On November 19, Logitech G, the company's gaming division, will host a live-streamed event at its San Jose headquarters to celebrate the occasion. This, likely coincidentally, aligns with the release day of GTA 6. It's unclear exactly what the event will feature, but it will be hosted by Logitech G’s general manager, Robin Piispannen.

“Whether diving into a game like GTA 6 or Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4, shaving seconds off lap times in Forza, or teaming up in an online battle, Game Day gives our team a shared purpose," he says. “We see firsthand how Logitech employees who sharpen their skills in-game translate directly back to work & problem solving.”

In Pictures: How GTA 6's Jason and Lucia Have Evolved Since 2023

GTA 6 is officially almost a week away from launch, and fans can officially preload the massive game starting today . Millions of people are expected to take the game's launch day off, and some countries are even advertising ways for people to do so . It's expected to be one of the biggest cultural events of the decade, if not the century. Rockstar hasn't revealed GTA 6's preorder data so far, but its parent company, Take-Two Interactive, has confirmed that they're "far in excess" of their expectations .

articles.title: IGN to Stream the 2027 New York Game Awards
articles.summary: The 2027 New York Game Awards are on the horizon, and IGN will once again be the official destination to stream the broadcast.
articles.body:
The 2027 New York Game Awards are on the horizon, and IGN will once again be the official destination to stream the broadcast.

The 16th annual New York Game Awards will take place on November 19, 2026, where legendary voice actor Troy Baker ( The Last of Us , Indiana Jones and the Great Circle ) will be recognized as the Andrew Yoon Legend Award recipient.

In honor of the late Andrew Yoon , a member and journalist in the New York Videogame Critics Circle, this award honors “game changers” in the industry who have “propelled the gaming world forward, celebrating their profound impact on an industry that continues to captivate and connect people worldwide.”

“When we consider our upcoming Andrew Yoon Legend winners, we’re looking for individuals who’ve made a deep cultural impact on the video game landscape, and Troy Baker felt like the perfect addition,” Harold Goldberg, co-founder and president, NYVGCC, said in a statement. “Troy is such a force of nature within the games industry. We’ve recognized his voice-acting performances at previous New York Game Awards, and we are ecstatic to have him join our roster of Andrew Yoon Legend winners. Plus, our audiences are in for a treat with his musical performance after this year's awards. You’ll only get to experience that moment in person at SVA Theatre!”

“It’s hard to find a video game from the past 10 or 20 years without mentioning Troy Baker,” Reggie Fils-Aimé, the former president of Nintendo of America and NYVGCC board member, added. “It’s because his performances are so ingrained in some of the most beloved video games in recent history, and he brought personality and meaning to those characters.”

“Troy is someone who has left a mark on our students, both through his work and during his time speaking with them ahead of the awards,” said Ryan O’Callaghan, executive director for NYVGCC. “We couldn’t ask for a better legend winner to celebrate our 16th annual New York Game Awards.”

After the awards, Troy Baker will perform a concert for in-person attendees, which all ticket holders are eligible to attend. Tickets are priced at $85 and can be purchased through Humanitix , with a limited number of VIP tickets available for $100. VIP tickets grant purchasers preferred seating during the awards, as well as access to the official after-party presented by New Blood Interactive.

As previously mentioned, the awards will be livestreamed on IGN’s website and YouTube channels, as well as the New York Videogame Critics Circle’s official social media channels.

Proceeds from this year’s New York Game Awards will benefit the NYVGCC’s Playing with Purpose writing program, which brings journalism classes and workshops, as well as courses in game narrative writing, to schools and shelters throughout New York City. Playing with Purpose received its first National Endowment for the Arts grant this year, which will help expand its classes to students in the Hudson Valley Middletown School District, as well as its work at the Lab School for Finance and Technology, and High School for Fashion Industries.

articles.title: Burger King Italy Gets Official Magic: The Gathering Meal With Whopper-Themed Deck Boxes
articles.summary: Burger King just launched a Magic: The Gathering meal that comes with Whopper-themed deck boxes and sleeves. Unfortunately, the promotion is exclusive to Burger King Italy, with no indication that it will expand to other countries.
articles.body:
Burger King just launched a Magic: The Gathering meal that comes with Whopper-themed deck boxes and sleeves. Unfortunately, the promotion is exclusive to Burger King Italy, with no indication that it will expand to other countries.

However, not all hope is lost for players from other regions — this is one of the first fast-food partnerships from Wizards of the Coast, following the trend of franchises like Pokémon . If the promotion goes well, it’s safe to expect more MTG collaborations across other regions in the future.

The Great Gathering Bundle (they use English on the official Burger King Italy site ) includes your choice of a Chicken Krispper, Double Cheeseburger, or the plant-based Impossible Whopper with fries and a drink. It’s priced at €19.90, equivalent to roughly $22 USD, and is available now through November 30.

That sounds yummy and all, but the real kicker that’s both intrigued and frustrated Magic fans is the new TCG accessories. Each meal comes with a Burger King-themed deck box and 100 card sleeves, perfect for your silliest Commander deck. Both accessories, which can be see in the image above, are designed in the style of a Whopper burger, with an orange ‘sesame bun’ pattern, a patty, and layers of toppings.

Sturdy deck boxes on their own are rarely under $20, making the accessories a genuinely good deal. As it stands, however, the only way to get your hands on them is by going to Italy to chow down on some Burger King.

Unlike the Pokémon Happy Meal , the MTG Burger King collaboration does not include any promotional cards. This could be a good thing, as region-locked cards can compound ongoing scalping concerns in an already tumultuous TCG market. Still, I wouldn’t be surprised if the Burger King deck boxes end up becoming a hot commodity on EBay.

Keen customers have already been sharing their spoils online, picking up some buzz from online MTG communities and the ire of fans from other countries. One X user who got their hands on the collab praises the quality of the deck box, but suggests the sleeves "feel a little flimsy and cheap."

The MTG collab being exclusive to Italy isn’t entirely random. As part of the collaboration, Burger King is sponsoring a number of local Pauper tournaments. The promotion is likely intended to help grow MTG’s audience in a new region, and Wizards appears to have a fond spot for the Pauper community in particular.

For now, most of us are stuck watching Magic fans enjoy the collab from afar, but content creators are on the case. articles.title: Spooked Mare - The Witcher 3 Guide - IGN
articles.summary: Spooked Mare is a unique Side Quest in The Witcher 3 that takes place outside the main city hub of the region, featuring a "woodland spook" and
articles.body:
Spooked Mare is a unique Side Quest in The Witcher 3 that takes place outside the main city hub of the region, featuring a "woodland spook" and horses. It's relatively quick, and while it may not be the most lucrative Side Quest in the area, there's still a small chunk of Crowns and experience to claim.

To help you make the best choice in Spooked Mare and finish the Side Quest quickly, here's IGN's guide, including which horse offers the best reward.

To start Spooked Mare, you'll need to head east of Oxenfurt and look for a villager standing in front of his home. He'll tell Geralt about a "woodland spook" that kidnapped his gray horse, and ask for help in getting the creature home.

Use your Witcher Senses at the home. You'll discover blood near the front gate and horse tracks.

Following the horse tracks, you'll end up at a Scoia'tael, up the way to the south east, where the mare can be found. Speaking to the Scoia'tael at the camp, you'll learn that there was an urgent need for horses to transport the people's wounded.

You have multiple ways of dealing with the situation here. Firstly, you can leave the horse here, but you'll forego any chance of a reward, failing the Side Quest.

You can also demand the horse back, with your options being:

Fighting the Scoia'tael in a relatively straightforward fight, utilizing Igni and Aard for extra damage

Bribing the Scoia'tael with 100 x Crowns

If you have the Crowns, the second option here is the best. If not, use Axii -- and if yours is too low-level, opt for the violent approach.

From here, you'll need to pick out the horse to take back to the villager. You can pick out the villager's gray mare, or you can bring back a different horse -- it's stronger and more lively, so you'll get a better reward.

When you've returned a horse to the villager, the Side Quest will wrap up.

If you returned the correct mare to the villager, you will get 20 x Crowns and 25 x experience. If you returned a younger horse, you will get 50 x Crowns and 25 x experience.

articles.title: We Build LEGO Downton Abbey, a Stately Set That's Worthy of the Crawley Name
articles.summary: We build LEGO Ideas Downton Abbey, a big, heavy, stately set that comes with 13 minifigures.
articles.body:
I like Julian Fellowes’ current HBO show The Gilded Age just fine, with its American characters’ focus on social striving and entrepreneurial success. But I suspect I'll always prefer Fellowes’ previous show, Downton Abbey. It’s a British historical drama that takes place as the era of landed aristocracy evolves into a more modern, fluid class structure. With its enormous cast of characters you want to root for – both the aristocratic Crawleys as well as the servants – watching Downton Abbey is like a warm hug.

I’ve seen the full run of Downton Abbey more than once – I’m talking all six seasons of the show, plus the three follow-up movies. I even recently bought the Ultimate Legacy Collection , which means another rewatch is likely in the near future (after the fourth season of The Gilded Age concludes, anyway).

During the hundred-plus hours I’ve spent in the company of the Crawleys and co., I’ve become intimately familiar with the rooms and architecture of the massive building of the title.

Downton Abbey is where the series’ massive cast of characters live and work. It’s where they clash with each other and make up (or don’t). It’s where they get sick and die (or get better). It’s where they fret about money, or get sent off to war, or make major life decisions that will affect their futures. It’s where they live their eventful early 20th-century lives.

The fictional building Downton Abbey is based on (and often filmed at) the very real Highclere Castle , which was built in 1679 in southern England. It’s a sprawling manor that has three full floors, with towers springing from the corners and center of the building.

LEGO Ideas Downton Abbey ( see it at LEGO ) stays true to the real castle’s design, but shrinks it down to minifigure scale, with just two main stories and the towers. Rather than depicting the entire building, which would likely be tedious to build and hide the interior rooms, the set focuses on the front facade. The back of the set is open to reveal six rooms anyone who’s watched the show would recognize.

Shrinking Downton Abbey down this way works beautifully. The exterior is finely detailed, with over a dozen windows, as well as downspouts, pinnacles, and an ornate heraldic stone portico over the entrance, just like the real castle.

Building such a large set took me many hours, over the course of a couple of weeks. It’s comprised of nearly 5,000 pieces, with the bricks divided into 35 bags and the building instructions separated into two books. Despite the time it takes, the build itself is generally enjoyable, especially when you’re making all the little furniture and items that bring the rooms to life.

Just like in the show, the interior of LEGO Downton Abbey are divided between the “upstairs,” where the Crawleys live and work, and the “downstairs,” where the domestic servants prepare the food and take their breaks. Upstairs are the Crawley’s dining room, main hall, and grand library. Downstairs are the kitchen, servants' hall, and the office of Carson the butler.

The set is large overall, but dividing two floors into six rooms means each room is relatively small. The LEGO designers have made the most of the space, packing lots of distinctive details into each area. Upstairs, the grand library alone has bookcases and curtains lining the walls, as well as a couch, a pot of flowers, a writing desk, and a fireplace. Downstairs, the servants’ hall has two rows of bells on one wall, just like you see in the opening credits of the show. In Carson’s office, his desk is adorned with a wine decanter, a lamp, and an old-school telephone. It’s always fun to see how just a few bricks can transform into an identifiable object in the house.

Since Downton Abbey has a notably large cast of characters, it’s only fitting that this LEGO set comes with a slew of minifigures. You get 13 in all, including most of the main characters we follow throughout the series. All of the women in dresses come with an alternate pair of legs that allow them to sit down as well.

The only part of the set that’s somewhat of a drag to build is the exterior walls, which are made of lots of repeated parts. This is a big, heavy set, and to sustain the weight, the walls have to be structurally sound. That means you have to build lots of the same thick, complex corner pieces to situate throughout the build. This is to be expected in a set based on a large building, but I found doing just a bag or two a day helped ward off the potential boredom.

Once the build is complete, the entire second story of the house can be lifted neatly off, giving you easy access to the lower interior rooms. The floors of both levels are sturdily built; they feel strong enough that you can move each story of the manor without worrying that the whole thing will fall apart in your hands.

The final piece of the build is the bench that sits under the cedar tree near the manor. In the show, you’ll often find Lady Mary sitting there, or the Dowager Countess.

I realize you have to be a pretty die-hard Downton Abbey fan to drop $349.99 on a LEGO set. But if you are, and you have the cash, you won't regret picking it up. It’s intricately designed, with lots of notable details from the show. It’s a largely enjoyable (if occasionally tedious) build, and the large cast of minifigures is delightful and full of personality. I enjoyed my time with this set as one more way to immerse myself in the world of Downton Abbey, at least until my next binge through the show.
